name: External breast expansion (Brava)

card.summary: A dome-shaped suction bra worn on the chest to stretch breast tissue and increase the volume a plastic surgeon can fill with fat grafting, aimed at a fuller bust without implants.
card.aka: vacuum expansion; external vacuum expansion (EVE); Brava; EVERA
card.note: Used mainly around fat-transfer surgery; the largest randomised trial interim analysis found no statistically significant difference versus no expansion.

quick.overview:
External breast expansion uses a pair of rigid domes that sit over the breasts and apply gentle, sustained suction. The aim is to stretch the tissue and encourage blood vessel growth so that the breast can hold more volume, giving a fuller bust without a silicone or saline implant.

The approach became best known as a way to prepare the chest for autologous fat transfer, where fat taken from elsewhere on the body is placed in the breast. Studies have measured volume and vessel changes with MRI, and a randomised trial of reconstruction patients has reported interim results comparing it with no expansion [1][2].
quick.how: The domes are worn for many hours a day over a period of weeks, typically before a fat-grafting operation and sometimes afterwards, as set out in surgical protocols and trials. Surgeons run it as part of a planned reconstruction or augmentation programme and often track volume with MRI.
quick.risks: Reported issues in the literature and from users include skin irritation, bruising, discomfort and the time burden of wearing the device for long daily periods. Fat graft survival is partial, so more than one session is often planned. Any plan involving surgery carries the usual operative risks and should be discussed with a plastic surgeon.

lead: External breast expansion, often called by the brand name Brava or described as external vacuum expansion (EVE), is a non-surgical technique in which dome-shaped cups attached to the chest apply low, continuous suction to the breasts. The aim is to enlarge the breast envelope and improve the blood supply so that more volume can be added, most often with fat transferred from the patient's own body.[1][2]

People interested in a larger or fuller bust without implants use it as part of an autologous fat-transfer plan. Wearing the device before surgery is intended to create room and a better recipient environment for the grafted fat, which tends to survive only in part, so surgeons commonly plan to overfill.[3]

Research includes an MRI study in Asian women that examined vessel count and density during expansion with the Brava device and a newer design,[2] a completed registered trial of a device called EVERA in women with small breasts,[4] and a multicentre randomised controlled trial in total breast reconstruction whose interim analysis reported no statistically significant difference in augmentation or graft retention between expansion and no expansion.[1]

chain: Blood vessel growth and a larger recipient space
More fat can be grafted and retained
angle.text: The device is used to enlarge the breast's capacity and prepare it for fat transfer, so the visible volume comes mainly from the graft. Users and surgeons describe it as a route to a fuller natural-feeling bust without implants.

paras: The system consists of two rigid domes joined to a soft seal around each breast and connected to a small pump or a self-regulating mechanism that holds a mild vacuum. It is worn under clothing for long periods so tissue is gradually expanded.[3]
Published protocols describe wearing a brassiere-like vacuum for around ten weeks in an early small study, and several weeks before fat grafting in reconstruction pathways.[3]

Surgeons use pre-expansion to enlarge the recipient site before fat is injected. Only a portion of injected fat survives at one year, so overfilling is common, and several grafting sessions spaced weeks apart may be planned.[3]
Registered trials have studied expansion in breast reconstruction after cancer treatment, including trials of external pre-expansion with fat transfer compared with standard therapy.[5][6]

A prospective trial in 34 Asian women used MRI to evaluate vessel count and density during external expansion, comparing the conventional Brava device with a second device.[2] A registered trial of the EVERA device in women with small breasts enrolled 34 participants and is listed as completed.[4]

The interim analysis of the multicentre EVE randomised trial included 53 women undergoing total breast reconstruction with three fat-transfer sessions. Mean augmentation was 190.7% with expansion and 176.4% without, and graft retention was 39.3% and 34.9%; neither difference was statistically significant at this stage, and quality-of-life results were not yet analysed.[1] Earlier smaller series summarised on Wikipedia reported volume gains of 60 to 200% at six months in 25 patients, with MRI data for only 12.[3]

The EVE trial assessed adverse events as secondary outcomes and discussed the treatment burden placed on women, since the device must be worn for many hours daily.[1] Fat transfer itself has variable graft survival and the usual surgical risks.

timeline.event: Series of vacuum pre-expansion followed by fat grafting reported 60 to 200% volume increases at six months in 25 patients.[3]
EVERA trial for small breasts begins (NCT02009137).[4]
Trial of external pre-expansion with fat transfer in breast reconstruction registered (NCT02339779).[5]
MRI study of vessel count and density during external expansion published.[2]
Interim results of the multicentre EVE randomised trial published.[1]
